A peril is the event that actually causes the loss, such as fire, flood or theft. A hazard is a condition that increases the chance or size of loss, like storing inflammable goods carelessly.
Which of the following is an example of a pure risk?
The chance that a factory may be damaged by a flood
Buying gold for trading in the hope of a quick profit
Purchasing a lottery ticket that may win a prize
Starting a new business that may earn a profit or make a loss
A pure risk offers only the possibility of loss or no loss, as with flood damage. The other options are speculative risks, which carry a chance of gain as well, and are normally not insurable.
A large company running hundreds of delivery vans decides to pay for minor dents and scratches out of its own funds instead of insuring them. This is:
Risk transfer
Risk avoidance
Risk reduction through loss prevention
Risk retention
When an organisation consciously bears small, predictable losses itself, it is retaining the risk. Transfer would mean buying insurance, while avoidance would mean not running the vans at all.
A restaurant stores cylinders of cooking gas and drums of kerosene right next to its open kitchen fire. This condition is an example of:
Moral hazard
Physical hazard
Speculative risk
Risk retention

A physical hazard is a tangible condition of the property or its surroundings that increases the chance of loss. Moral hazard, in contrast, relates to the attitude or dishonesty of the insured person.
Insurers can estimate their likely claims for the coming year with reasonable accuracy mainly because of:
The principle of subrogation applied to every claim
The law of large numbers
The fact that every insured person will definitely suffer a loss
Government guarantees on all insurance losses
When a large number of similar, independent exposures are pooled, actual losses tend to come close to expected losses. This law of large numbers lets insurers price risk and fix premiums sensibly.
Which of the following is an example of the secondary burden of risk?
The cost of rebuilding a shop that has actually been destroyed by fire
The value of stock stolen in a burglary at a godown
The loss of a car that was written off in an accident
Keeping large sums idle as a reserve to meet a possible future loss
The primary burden is the actual loss suffered. The secondary burden includes costs borne even if no loss occurs, such as funds locked up as reserves and the fear and anxiety of uncertainty.
A homeowner insures his house because its destruction would leave him financially ruined. Which rule of risk management is he following?
Don't risk more than you can afford to lose
Don't risk a lot for a little
Consider the likely outcomes carefully
Avoid every activity that carries any risk at all

The rule of not risking more than you can afford to lose says that a loss which would cause financial ruin must be transferred. 'Don't risk a lot for a little' is about weighing premium against cover.
An insurer that has accepted a very large refinery risk passes a part of it to another insurer under a separate contract, without involving the policyholder. This arrangement is:
Double insurance
Contribution
Reinsurance
Assignment

Reinsurance is insurance bought by an insurer to share a part of its own risk. The policyholder deals only with the original insurer. Double insurance is when the insured buys cover from two insurers for the same risk.

Customer Service & Grievances.overview: This chapter deals with the agent's role in serving customers before and after the sale. It covers the importance of service for an intangible product like insurance, the dimensions of service quality (reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness), moments of truth, and communication skills such as active listening and body language. It also explains how grievances are handled: the insurer's own grievance cell, IRDAI's grievance system, the Insurance Ombudsman and consumer commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Focus on how an agent should behave in real situations and on the order in which a complaint moves through the redressal forums.
questions: Active listening by an insurance agent mainly involves:
Talking continuously about the product's many features so that there is never any awkward silence in the meeting
Preparing the next sales pitch while the customer is still speaking
Agreeing with every statement of the customer to avoid any disagreement
Paying full attention to the customer, clarifying doubts and responding to what is actually said

Active listening means concentrating on the speaker, asking clarifying questions and responding to their real concerns. It builds trust and helps the agent understand the customer's needs before suggesting a product.
In the language of customer service, a 'moment of truth' refers to:
The day on which the insurer finally settles and pays a claim after completing all its investigations
The time when the agent discloses his commission
Any point of contact at which the customer forms an impression of the service
The final signature on the proposal form
A moment of truth is every interaction — a phone call, a visit, a receipt — where the customer judges the quality of service. A claim payment is one such moment, but not the only one.
An agent always delivers policy documents, premium reminders and claim forms exactly when he has promised. Which dimension of service quality does this mainly reflect?
Tangibles
Reliability
Empathy
Assurance

Reliability is the ability to perform the promised service dependably and accurately. Tangibles relate to physical appearance, empathy to individual care, and assurance to knowledge and courtesy that inspire confidence.
Under the Insurance Ombudsman mechanism, an award passed by the Ombudsman is:
Binding on the insurer once the complainant accepts it, while the complainant may instead pursue other remedies
Binding on the complainant but only advisory for the insurer
Advisory for both parties, and enforceable against the insurer only after it has been separately approved and notified by IRDAI
Binding on both parties, with no further remedy available to anyone

The Ombudsman's award binds the insurer, which must comply within the prescribed time once the complainant accepts it. A complainant who is not satisfied is free to reject it and approach other forums such as a consumer commission.
A policyholder who alleges deficiency in service by an insurer can file a complaint before a Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under:
Section 41 of the Insurance Act, 1938
The Indian Contract Act, 1872
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019
The Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956

Insurance is a 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, so policyholders can approach District, State or National Commissions for deficiency in service. The other Acts do not set up consumer forums.
Which of the following is a sign of positive body language when an agent meets a prospect?
Comfortable eye contact and an open, relaxed posture
Arms folded tightly across the chest throughout the meeting
Frequently checking the mobile phone while the prospect speaks
Looking away and tapping fingers on the table
Steady eye contact and an open posture show attention, honesty and confidence. Folded arms, checking the phone or fidgeting send signals of disinterest or defensiveness and weaken trust.
A customer telephones the agent, very angry because his claim has been delayed. The agent's best first response is to:
Tell the customer that claim delays are the insurer's fault, not his, and end the call
Advise the customer to file a court case immediately
Argue that the customer must have submitted wrong documents
Listen patiently, acknowledge the problem and promise a specific follow-up

An upset customer first needs to be heard. Acknowledging the problem and committing to a definite follow-up calms the situation and preserves the relationship; blaming others or arguing usually worsens the complaint.
Why is good service especially important in selling insurance compared with selling most physical goods?
Insurance products are identical across all insurers, so price is irrelevant
Insurance is an intangible promise, so the service experienced is what the customer actually judges
IRDAI fixes exactly the same premium for every policy of every insurer, so the only thing left to compete on is service
Customers buy insurance only once in their lifetime and never renew it
A customer cannot see or touch an insurance policy; he experiences it only through the service he receives and the claim at the end. Strong service builds trust, renewals and referrals.

Regulatory Aspects of Agency.overview: This chapter covers the legal framework within which an insurance agent works. It explains the role of IRDAI, set up under the IRDA Act, 1999, and key provisions of the Insurance Act, 1938, such as payment of commission only to authorised persons and the prohibition of rebating. It also covers the agent's code of conduct: disclosing identity and the insurer represented, explaining product features honestly, avoiding mis-selling, handling premiums properly and helping customers with documentation and claims. Learners should know the grounds on which an agency can be cancelled and should be able to recognise ethical and unethical behaviour in practical situations.
questions: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) was established under:
The Insurance Act, 1938
The IRDA Act, 1999
The LIC Act, 1956
The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972
IRDAI is a statutory body created by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999. The Insurance Act, 1938 is the main law governing insurance business, which IRDAI administers.
Under Section 40 of the Insurance Act, 1938, an insurer is NOT permitted to pay commission or remuneration for procuring business to:
An individual agent appointed by the insurer
A corporate agent registered with IRDAI
An insurance broker licensed by IRDAI and acting on behalf of the client who placed the business
A person who is not an agent or intermediary authorised under the Act
Section 40 allows commission only to persons authorised to solicit insurance, such as appointed agents and licensed intermediaries. Paying an unlicensed person for bringing in business is prohibited.
Which of the following is the most likely ground for cancellation of an individual agent's appointment?
Being found to have suppressed material facts or committed fraud while soliciting business
Selling more policies than the agent's annual target
Recommending a pure term plan instead of a savings-oriented endowment plan to a young customer with dependants and a home loan
Advising a customer to update his nomination after marriage

An insurer may cancel an agent's appointment for misconduct such as fraud, misrepresentation or breach of the code of conduct. Meeting targets or giving suitable advice are good practices, not grounds for cancellation.
Under the code of conduct, while soliciting business an agent must:
Keep the name of his insurer confidential until the policy is issued
Promise a fixed bonus rate for all future years
Identify himself and disclose the name of the insurer he represents
Collect the proposal without explaining the product features

The code of conduct requires an agent to disclose his identity and licence, the insurer he represents and, on request, his commission. He must explain product features honestly and must not promise future bonuses.
An agent describes a market-linked ULIP to a retired person seeking guaranteed monthly income as 'a fixed deposit with free insurance'. This is:
Acceptable, because a ULIP does have an insurance element
Acceptable, if the customer signs the proposal form
Rebating under Section 41 of the Insurance Act
Mis-selling through misrepresentation of the product

Describing a market-linked product as a guaranteed deposit misrepresents its risk and does not suit the customer's need. This is mis-selling. Rebating, in contrast, means sharing commission or premium as an inducement.
An agent's commission on a policy is paid by:
The policyholder, as a separate fee over and above the premium
IRDAI, from the fees collected from insurers
The insurer, out of the premium it receives
The Insurance Council, from its annual budget

Agents are remunerated by the insurer, and the cost of commission is built into the premium loading. The policyholder does not pay a separate fee to the agent, and neither IRDAI nor the Council pays commission.
A customer hands over the renewal premium in cash to his agent. As a matter of proper conduct, the agent should:
Keep it with him until the end of the grace period to earn interest
Deposit it with the insurer promptly and ensure the customer gets the insurer's official receipt
Give the customer a handwritten personal receipt on his own letterhead in place of the insurer's official premium receipt
Adjust part of it against his own commission before depositing
Premium belongs to the insurer and must be remitted promptly; only the insurer's receipt is valid proof of payment. Holding the money or deducting commission from it is a serious breach of conduct.
If a proposer is unable to fill in the proposal form himself, the agent may help by:
Filling it as per the proposer's answers, explaining the contents, and obtaining the proposer's signature with a suitable declaration
Filling and signing the form on the proposer's behalf without telling him the contents
Leaving the medical questions blank so that underwriting is quicker
Writing down the answers that he believes the underwriter is most likely to accept, even where the proposer actually said something different

The proposal remains the proposer's statement. If someone else fills it, the contents must be explained to the proposer, who signs it, and a declaration to this effect is recorded. Altering or omitting answers is unethical.

Legal Principles of Insurance.overview: This chapter covers the legal foundations of an insurance contract. It begins with the elements of a valid contract under the Indian Contract Act — offer and acceptance, consideration, free consent, competent parties and lawful object — and the difference between void and voidable contracts. It then explains the special principles of insurance: utmost good faith and material facts, insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, contribution and proximate cause. Learners should also understand warranties and representations. Expect scenario questions where you must decide which principle applies and whether a loss is payable.
questions: A storm blows the roof off a warehouse and rain then enters and spoils the goods inside. The policy covers storm but excludes rain damage. The loss to the goods is:
Not payable, because rain was the last cause in time
Payable only up to half, because two causes were involved
Payable, because the storm is the proximate cause of the damage
Not payable, because a warehouse cannot be insured against storm
Proximate cause is the active, efficient cause that sets the chain of events in motion. The storm caused the rain to enter, so the storm is the proximate cause and the loss is covered.
After paying a full own-damage claim, a motor insurer files a suit against the negligent truck owner who caused the accident to recover the amount. This right arises from the principle of:
Subrogation
Contribution
Utmost good faith
Proximate cause

Subrogation transfers the insured's rights against a third party to the insurer after it has paid the loss, preventing the insured from being paid twice. Contribution concerns sharing a loss between insurers.
Which of the following would be a material fact for a life insurance proposal?
The proposer's favourite sport is cricket
The proposer recently changed his mobile handset and telephone service provider
The proposer prefers vegetarian food on weekdays
The proposer underwent heart bypass surgery two years ago
A material fact is one that would influence the underwriter's decision to accept the risk or the premium charged. A past heart surgery clearly affects mortality risk; the other facts are irrelevant.
In the formation of an insurance contract, the 'offer' is usually made by:
The insurer, by publishing its sales brochure and advertisements
The proposer, by submitting a signed proposal form
The agent, by giving a premium quotation
IRDAI, by approving the product
A brochure or quotation is only an invitation to offer. The proposer makes the offer through the proposal form, and the insurer accepts it, often with or without modifications, by issuing the policy.
A contract entered into because one party's consent was obtained by undue influence is:
Void from the very beginning and therefore unenforceable by either party
Voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so obtained
Valid and fully enforceable against both parties
Illegal and punishable as a criminal offence
Under the Indian Contract Act, consent caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation is not free, and the contract becomes voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.
Who among the following has an insurable interest in the life of a person?
A close neighbour who has lived in the same housing society for many years
A fan who admires that person's public work
A colleague who works in another department
A bank that has lent money to that person, to the extent of the loan
Insurable interest exists where a person would suffer a financial loss from the death of the life assured. A creditor has such interest up to the debt amount; a neighbour, fan or colleague does not.
A term in a policy that must be strictly complied with, whether or not it is material to the risk, and whose breach allows the insurer to avoid the policy, is a:
Warranty
Representation
Endorsement
Recital clause

A warranty is a promise by the insured that must be literally fulfilled. A breach entitles the insurer to avoid the contract even if the breach did not contribute to the loss. A representation only needs to be substantially true.
In an insurance contract, the consideration given by the insured is the:
Sum assured
Proposal form
Premium
Policy document

Consideration is what each party gives in exchange. The insured pays the premium, and the insurer gives its promise to pay on the happening of the insured event. The sum assured is the insurer's promised payment.

Life Insurance & Financial Planning.overview: This chapter links life insurance with personal financial planning. It explains life stages and how needs change from a young single earner to retirement, the need-based approach to finding the right amount of cover, and the role of life insurance as a unique asset that creates an immediate estate. It also covers basic financial concepts: the time value of money, compounding, inflation, the risk-return trade-off among asset classes, liquidity and emergency funds. Practise simple calculations such as future value under inflation and the cover gap, and always start from the customer's goals before suggesting any product.
questions: A couple whose children are now financially independent, and who have about ten years left until retirement, should usually give priority to:
Buying the largest possible child education plan
Taking a new long-tenure home loan to buy a second house for investment
Investing all savings in a single high-risk small-cap stock
Building a retirement corpus and ensuring adequate health cover
In the 'empty nest' stage, family protection needs reduce while retirement and health needs grow. Building a retirement corpus and securing health cover are the main goals for this life stage.
If inflation averages 6% per annum, an annual household expense of ₹50,000 today will cost approximately how much after 12 years?
Future cost = 50,000 × (1.06)^12 ≈ ₹1,00,610. ₹86,000 wrongly applies simple growth (6% × 12 years), while ₹89,542 and ₹1,06,646 compound for 10 and 13 years respectively.
Before recommending any insurance product, an agent should first:
Show the product with the highest commission
Understand the customer's goals, income, liabilities and existing cover
Collect the first premium so that the customer does not change his mind
Compare competitor products only on the basis of premium
Need-based selling begins with fact-finding: goals, income, dependants, loans and current cover. Only after this analysis can a suitable product and sum assured be recommended.
Over a long period, which of these asset classes typically carries the highest risk along with the highest expected return?
Equity shares
Bank savings account
Bank fixed deposit
Government of India bonds held to maturity
Equity offers higher expected long-term returns but with high volatility. Savings accounts, fixed deposits and government bonds held to maturity provide lower but more stable and predictable returns.
Life insurance is often called a unique asset because:
It always gives the highest return among all available investments, including equity shares and property
Its value can never be affected by lapse or surrender
It creates an immediate estate for the family as soon as the policy is in force
It can be bought only by people with very high incomes
Ordinary savings build up slowly, but a life policy guarantees the full sum assured to the family from the first premium if death occurs. This 'instant estate' is what makes life insurance unique.
An emergency fund for meeting sudden expenses should preferably be kept in:
Liquid, low-risk instruments such as a savings account or a liquid fund
Real estate, because property prices generally rise
Long-term deposits that carry a heavy penalty for premature withdrawal before maturity
Small-cap equity shares to maximise returns
An emergency fund must be available quickly without loss of value, so liquidity and safety matter most. Property, locked-in deposits and volatile equities are unsuitable for this purpose.

Rakesh has a home loan outstanding of ₹20 lakh, expects children's education costs of ₹15 lakh, and needs a family income corpus of ₹40 lakh. He already has life cover of ₹25 lakh and savings of ₹10 lakh. Using the needs approach, his additional life cover requirement is:
₹75 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹65 lakh
₹40 lakh
Total needs = 20 + 15 + 40 = ₹75 lakh. Less existing cover (₹25 lakh) and savings (₹10 lakh) gives a gap of ₹40 lakh. ₹75 lakh ignores existing resources; ₹50 lakh ignores savings.
₹1,00,000 invested at 8% per annum compounded annually will grow in 3 years to approximately:
Maturity value = 1,00,000 × (1.08)^3 = ₹1,25,971. ₹1,24,000 is the simple-interest figure, and ₹1,16,640 is the value after only two years of compounding.

Life Insurance Products.overview: This chapter describes the main types of life insurance products sold in India. It covers term plans and their variants (return of premium, decreasing term for loans), whole life, endowment and money-back plans, participating and non-participating policies, bonuses, unit-linked plans, annuities (immediate and deferred), and riders such as accidental death benefit. Learners should be able to match a product to a customer's need, understand how a ULIP allocates premium into units, and calculate simple reversionary bonus. Focus on the differences between traditional and unit-linked plans and between protection and savings products.
questions: A whole life policy pays the sum assured:
Only if the insured survives a fixed term of 20 years
On the death of the insured whenever it occurs (or at a very high specified age)
Only on death caused by an accident
In equal instalments every five years during the term, with the balance paid on survival to maturity
Whole life insurance provides cover for the entire lifetime, so the claim arises on death whenever it happens; many plans also pay at a high age such as 99 or 100.
In a participating (with-profits) life policy, the policyholder:
Bears the full investment risk through units
Receives no benefit other than the guaranteed sum assured
Must participate in the insurer's board meetings
Shares in the insurer's surplus through bonuses

Participating policies share in the surplus of the insurer's par fund, usually through reversionary or terminal bonuses. Non-participating policies offer only the guaranteed benefits, and ULIPs pass investment risk to the policyholder.
Term insurance with return of premium (TROP) differs from a pure term plan mainly because:
The premiums paid are returned if the insured survives the policy term
It pays double the sum assured on death due to any cause during the policy term
It does not require any medical underwriting
It has no fixed policy term
Under TROP, the total premiums paid are refunded on survival to maturity, while a pure term plan pays nothing on survival. For this extra benefit, TROP premiums are noticeably higher.
A borrower wants life cover that reduces in line with his outstanding home loan. The most suitable product is:
A whole life policy
An immediate annuity
Mortgage redemption (decreasing term) assurance
A money-back policy with survival benefits every five years
Mortgage redemption assurance is a decreasing term plan whose sum assured falls roughly with the loan balance, so the loan can be cleared if the borrower dies. It is cheaper than a level term plan.
In a ULIP, an annual premium of ₹50,000 is paid. The premium allocation charge is 5% and the NAV on the date of allocation is ₹20. How many units are allotted?
Amount invested = 50,000 − 5% = ₹47,500. Units = 47,500 ÷ 20 = 2,375. 2,500 ignores the allocation charge, while 2,250 and 2,425 apply the charge incorrectly.
An accidental death benefit rider attached to a life policy:
Replaces the base sum assured on natural death
Refunds all premiums if no accident occurs
Pays an additional sum if death results from an accident
Covers hospitalisation expenses for any illness
A rider is an add-on to the base policy. The accidental death benefit rider pays an extra amount, over the base sum assured, if death is caused by an accident within the conditions of the rider.
In a deferred annuity, the annuity payments:
Begin immediately, one period after the single premium is paid
Begin after a chosen deferment period during which the purchase money accumulates
Are paid only to the nominee after the annuitant's death, together with all the accumulated interest
Are paid only once, as a lump sum on retirement
A deferred annuity has an accumulation phase, after which income begins at the vesting date. In an immediate annuity, payments start straight away, from the end of the first payment period.
A simple reversionary bonus of ₹45 per thousand sum assured is declared on a policy with a sum assured of ₹4,00,000. The bonus added to the policy for that year is:
Bonus = 45 × (4,00,000 ÷ 1,000) = 45 × 400 = ₹18,000. Simple reversionary bonus is calculated on the basic sum assured only and is added to the policy, payable with the claim.

Pricing & Valuation.overview: This chapter explains how life insurance premiums are calculated and how insurers value their liabilities. The net premium depends on mortality and interest, while the office premium adds loadings for expenses, contingencies and bonus. Learners should understand the level premium system and why it builds reserves, the effect of age, sum assured and payment mode on premium, and rebates. Valuation by actuaries compares liabilities with assets to find surplus, which in participating business is distributed as bonus. Focus on the direction in which each factor moves the premium, and on simple premium calculations per thousand sum assured.
questions: The net premium of a life insurance policy is calculated mainly on the basis of:
Mortality, interest and agent's commission
Expenses and expected bonus
Mortality and interest
Taxes and the insurer's profit target

Net (pure) premium reflects only expected mortality cost discounted at an assumed rate of interest. Loadings for expenses, commission, contingencies and bonus are added later to arrive at the office premium.
Other things being equal, the premium for a term plan for a 45-year-old is higher than for a 25-year-old because:
The probability of death rises with age
Older people are always charged a penalty by IRDAI
The interest rate assumed is lower for older people
Commission rates are higher for older proposers
Mortality tables show the probability of death increasing with age. Since the cost of providing cover depends on this probability, the premium for an older life is higher.
Under the level premium system, the premiums paid in the early years of a policy are:
Less than the actual cost of risk, with the resulting deficit being recovered from the insurer's shareholders in later years
Exactly equal to the cost of risk in each year
Refunded to the policyholder at the end of each year
More than the actual cost of risk, the excess building a reserve for later years
With a level premium, the policyholder pays the same amount every year. In early years, this exceeds the cost of mortality; the surplus builds a reserve that meets the higher risk of later years.
Actuarial valuation of a life insurer is carried out mainly to:
Fix the commission of each agent
Compare its liabilities with its assets and determine surplus or deficit
Decide the premium for a single new policy
Calculate the income tax payable by each policyholder on the maturity proceeds of his policy
Valuation estimates the present value of future policy liabilities and compares it with assets. The resulting surplus, if any, helps decide bonus to participating policyholders and confirms solvency.
Life insurers often give a rebate in premium for a higher sum assured because:
Larger policies have no mortality risk
Administrative costs per policy do not rise in proportion to the sum assured
IRDAI requires every insurer to give a fixed discount on all policies with a sum assured above ₹1 lakh
Agents are not paid any commission on large policies

Many policy costs, such as issuing documents and maintaining records, are similar for small and large policies. Spread over a bigger sum assured, the expense per thousand falls, and the saving is passed on as a rebate.
Over a year, the total premium under the annual mode is usually lower than under the monthly mode because:
Monthly-mode policyholders have higher mortality
Monthly premiums attract goods and services tax, whereas annual premiums are fully exempt from any such tax levy
Annual-mode policies do not carry any insurance cover
The insurer saves on collection costs and earns interest on the money for a longer period

Collecting premium once a year costs less, and the insurer receives the full year's money in advance, earning interest on it. Hence annual mode is cheaper, and monthly or quarterly modes carry a loading.
The tabular premium for a plan is ₹48 per thousand sum assured, and a rebate of ₹2 per thousand applies for the sum assured chosen. What is the annual premium for a sum assured of ₹5,00,000?
Net rate = 48 − 2 = ₹46 per thousand. Premium = 46 × 500 = ₹23,000. ₹24,000 ignores the rebate, while ₹22,000 deducts it twice.
In a life insurer's participating fund, surplus arises mainly when:
More policyholders lapse their policies after one year
The insurer raises its premium rates retrospectively
Actual experience of mortality, interest and expenses is better than assumed
Claims are delayed beyond the stipulated time

Premiums are based on cautious assumptions. If fewer people die, investments earn more, or expenses are lower than assumed, a surplus emerges, part of which is distributed to participating policyholders as bonus.

Documentation & Underwriting.overview: This chapter covers the documents used at each stage of a life policy and the process of underwriting. Documents include the prospectus, proposal form, age and KYC proof, first premium receipt, the policy document and endorsements. Learners should know standard and non-standard age proofs, the rules on nomination (including appointees for minor nominees) and assignment. Underwriting is the process of assessing and classifying risk: financial underwriting to avoid over-insurance, medical underwriting, and the treatment of standard and substandard lives. Focus on what each document proves and on recognising which factors an underwriter will look at closely.
questions: Among these documents, which one would an insurer normally regard as weaker, non-standard evidence of the proposer's age?
A passport
A birth certificate issued by the municipal registrar of births
A school leaving certificate
A self-declaration or affidavit of age

Non-standard age proofs, such as an affidavit or self-declaration, are less reliable, and insurers may accept them only with restrictions or an extra premium. Birth certificates, passports and school certificates are standard proofs.
The prospectus or sales brochure of a life insurance product must contain:
Only the insurer's past bonus rates and claim figures
Only the name and contact details of the agent
The product's features, benefits, exclusions and main terms and conditions
A guarantee that the product will always outperform bank fixed deposits over every policy term
The prospectus is meant to help a prospect make an informed decision, so it must describe the scope of benefits, conditions and exclusions honestly. It cannot promise returns that are not guaranteed.
The First Premium Receipt (FPR) issued by a life insurer signifies that:
The proposal is still under consideration
The insurance contract has commenced
The policy has been assigned to a bank
The free-look period has expired
The FPR is issued once the proposal is accepted and the first premium is adjusted. It is evidence that the contract has started; subsequent premiums are acknowledged through renewal premium receipts.
A change in the policyholder's address on an existing life policy is usually recorded by means of:
An endorsement
A fresh proposal form
A new policy bond
A revival quotation
Endorsements are written amendments that record changes in the terms or details of a policy after issue, such as address, nomination or plan changes. They form part of the policy document.
A proposer with a modest declared income asks for a very large sum assured without any apparent financial need. The underwriter's main concern here is:
The proposer's age proof being non-standard
The premium mode chosen by the proposer
Over-insurance and the possibility of moral hazard
The agent's eligibility for commission

Financial underwriting checks that the sum assured is reasonable relative to income and need. Excessive cover without justification suggests speculation or moral hazard, so the underwriter may limit the cover.
Under Section 39 of the Insurance Act, a nomination can be made by:
A policyholder who has taken a policy on his or her own life
Any person who pays the premium on someone else's life
The nominee, on behalf of the policyholder
The agent, at the time of collecting the proposal
Nomination is permitted only where the policyholder has insured his or her own life. It names who will receive the claim money. It can be made at proposal stage or later, by an endorsement.
When a policyholder nominates his minor son, he should also name:
An assignee who will become the owner of the policy
A guarantor who will continue paying the premium
A trustee under the Married Women's Property Act, 1874, to hold the policy money for the minor
An appointee to receive the claim money during the nominee's minority
A minor cannot give a valid discharge for the claim. So the policyholder names an appointee, who receives the policy money on the minor's behalf if the claim arises before the nominee turns 18.
Which of the following is most likely to make an underwriter ask for a detailed medical examination, even for a modest sum assured?
The proposer being a salaried employee of a government bank
A history of diabetes and high blood pressure disclosed in the proposal
The proposer choosing the annual mode of premium payment
The proposer having submitted a passport as age proof

Disclosed medical conditions such as diabetes or hypertension directly affect mortality, so the underwriter needs medical evidence to classify the life as standard or substandard. The other facts do not raise health concerns.

Life Insurance Claims.overview: This chapter explains how life insurance claims are settled. It distinguishes maturity, survival benefit, surrender and death claims, and lists the documents needed for each, such as the discharge voucher, policy document, death certificate, claimant's statement and, in unnatural deaths, the FIR and post-mortem report. It also covers who receives the money — nominee, assignee or legal heirs — the treatment of loans and unpaid premiums, death during the grace period, and the grounds on which a claim may be repudiated. Practise calculating the net claim amount after deductions and know why early claims are examined more closely.
questions: For settling a maturity claim, the insurer normally requires:
A death certificate issued by the local municipal authority
A signed discharge voucher together with the original policy document and bank and KYC details
A First Information Report lodged with the police, along with the post-mortem report and the police inquest report
A fresh medical examination of the policyholder

A maturity claim is paid to the policyholder on survival to the end of the term. The insurer needs a discharge form, the policy document and payment details; death documents or medicals are irrelevant here.
Under a money-back policy, a survival benefit is paid:
Only when the insured dies during the term
Only when the policy is surrendered
Each year as a fixed percentage of the premium paid
When the insured survives to specified dates during the policy term
Money-back plans pay a portion of the sum assured at fixed intervals if the life assured is alive on those dates. These are survival benefits and are separate from the maturity and death benefits.

A policy has a sum assured of ₹5,00,000 and accrued bonus of ₹60,000. On the policyholder's death, there is an outstanding policy loan of ₹1,20,000 with unpaid interest of ₹8,000. The net claim payable is:
Claim = 5,00,000 + 60,000 − 1,20,000 − 8,000 = ₹4,32,000. ₹4,40,000 ignores the interest, and ₹5,60,000 ignores the loan altogether. The insurer recovers the loan and interest from the claim.
Which document is essential for any death claim under a life policy?
The maturity discharge voucher
The original proposal form
The death certificate
The agent's licence copy
A death claim cannot be settled without proof of death, normally the death certificate issued by the local authority, along with the claim form and the claimant's identity and bank details.
For an accidental death benefit claim, in addition to the usual death claim papers, the insurer generally requires:
A certificate from the employer only
The original age proof of the nominee
A fresh proposal form signed by the nominee
The FIR, post-mortem report and police inquest report
Since the benefit depends on death being accidental, the insurer needs police and medical records — FIR, inquest and post-mortem reports — to establish the cause and circumstances of death.
If a policyholder dies without a valid nomination or assignment, the claim amount is generally paid to:
The agent who sold the policy, to be distributed later
The insurer's unclaimed amounts fund, immediately
The legal heirs, on production of evidence of title such as a succession certificate
The policyholder's employer

Without a nominee or assignee, the insurer pays the persons legally entitled to the estate. It asks for evidence of title, such as a succession certificate or legal heir certificate, to obtain a valid discharge.
Within three years of the policy, a death claim may be repudiated mainly if the insurer can establish:
That the agent's licence had expired
Fraud or suppression of material facts in the proposal
That the nominee lives in another state
That the claim was submitted within the prescribed time

Under Section 45, a policy can be questioned within three years on grounds of fraud or misstatement or suppression of material facts. Administrative issues such as the agent's licence or nominee's address are not grounds.
If the life assured dies during the grace period without having paid the due premium, the insurer will usually:
Pay the claim after deducting the unpaid premium
Reject the claim because the premium was unpaid
Pay only the surrender value of the policy
Pay only the premiums received so far
During the grace period the policy remains in force. If death occurs then, the claim is admitted and the unpaid premium due is deducted from the claim amount.

Health Insurance.overview: This chapter covers health insurance products and their key features. It explains indemnity hospitalisation policies, family floaters, top-up and super top-up covers, critical illness and other fixed-benefit plans, and the inclusion of day-care procedures, AYUSH treatment and pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses. Learners should understand terms such as sum insured, sub-limits, room-rent limits with proportionate deduction, co-payment, deductibles, waiting periods and exclusions. Practise calculations on super top-ups and proportionate deduction, and be clear on the difference between indemnity and benefit policies. Avoid memorising limits that may change; focus on the concepts.
questions: A super top-up health policy differs from a regular top-up policy because its deductible applies to:
Each separate hospitalisation claim individually
Only claims made in the first year
The total of all admissible claims in a policy year
Only the pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses
A regular top-up pays only when a single claim exceeds the deductible. A super top-up considers the aggregate of claims in the year, paying once the combined amount crosses the deductible.
A super top-up policy has a deductible of ₹3 lakh. During the policy year, the insured has two admissible hospitalisation claims of ₹2 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh. The super top-up insurer will pay:
₹1.5 lakh
Nil
₹4.5 lakh
₹2 lakh
Aggregate claims = 2 + 2.5 = ₹4.5 lakh. Excess over the ₹3 lakh deductible = ₹1.5 lakh. A regular top-up with a per-claim deductible would pay nil, as neither single claim exceeds ₹3 lakh.
A family floater health policy provides:
A separate, equal sum insured for each family member, which cannot be shared with any other member
Cover only for the eldest member of the family
Cover for the family only while travelling abroad
One sum insured that can be used by any one or all of the covered family members

Under a floater, the sum insured 'floats' across the family: any member can use it, and total claims by all members cannot exceed it in the year. Individual policies give each person a separate sum insured.
A critical illness policy typically pays:
Only the actual hospital bills, up to the sum insured
A lump sum on diagnosis of a listed illness, irrespective of actual expenses
A fixed daily allowance for each day spent in hospital, subject to a maximum number of days
Only the cost of medicines after discharge

Critical illness cover is a benefit policy. On diagnosis of a covered illness such as cancer or a heart attack, and survival of any stated period, it pays a fixed lump sum regardless of the bills incurred.
The cost of diagnostic tests done a few days before admission, for the same illness for which the insured is hospitalised, is covered under:
Domiciliary hospitalisation
Pre-hospitalisation expenses
Day-care treatment
Post-hospitalisation expenses
Pre-hospitalisation cover pays for related medical expenses incurred for a specified number of days before admission. Post-hospitalisation cover applies to expenses after discharge.

A policy allows room rent of ₹5,000 per day, but the insured chooses a room costing ₹10,000 per day. Associated medical expenses to which proportionate deduction applies are ₹80,000. The amount payable for these expenses is:

The eligible room is half the room taken (5,000 ÷ 10,000), so associated expenses are paid proportionately: 80,000 × 0.5 = ₹40,000. Items such as pharmacy and implants are excluded from proportionate deduction.
AYUSH treatment covered under many health policies refers to:
Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy
Allopathy, Yoga, Unani, Surgery and Homoeopathy
Acupuncture, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Hydrotherapy
Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa and Herbal remedies only
AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy. Health policies cover in-patient treatment under these systems in recognised hospitals, subject to policy terms.
Day-care procedures in health insurance are:
Routine outpatient consultations with a general physician
Treatments taken only at home on a doctor's advice
Treatments that need less than 24 hours of hospitalisation because of advanced technology, and are covered
Cosmetic procedures done in a clinic in a single day
Procedures such as cataract surgery or chemotherapy can now be done in under 24 hours. Policies cover listed day-care procedures even though the usual 24-hour hospitalisation condition is not met.

General Insurance.overview: This chapter introduces the main lines of general (non-life) insurance. It covers fire and special perils policies and the basis of claim settlement (market value or reinstatement value), burglary, motor insurance (third-party liability and own damage, deductibles and salvage), marine hull and cargo, liability covers such as public liability, and miscellaneous covers like fidelity guarantee. Learners should know which perils are typically covered or excluded, how deductibles and salvage reduce a claim, and which policy suits a given business need. Focus on applying general insurance principles, especially indemnity, to practical claim situations.
questions: Which of the following is typically covered under a standard fire and special perils policy?
Gradual wear and tear of machinery
Loss due to war or invasion
Theft without any fire or other insured event
Damage caused by lightning
Lightning is a named peril under the standard fire and special perils policy. Wear and tear, war and simple theft are excluded or need separate covers such as burglary insurance.
A private car's own-damage loss is assessed at ₹38,000. The damaged parts, retained by the insured, have a salvage value of ₹2,000, and the compulsory deductible is ₹1,000. The claim payable is:

Claim = 38,000 − 2,000 (salvage retained by insured) − 1,000 (compulsory deductible) = ₹35,000. Paying ₹36,000 or ₹37,000 would ignore one of the deductions, giving the insured more than an indemnity.
A standard burglary policy usually requires, for a claim to be admissible:
That the theft was committed by an employee of the insured
Forcible and violent entry into or exit from the insured premises
That the stolen goods were kept outside the premises
That the loss occurred during a fire at the premises
Burglary insurance covers theft involving forcible and violent entry or exit. Theft by employees is excluded (fidelity guarantee covers it), and goods outside the premises are generally not covered.
Marine hull insurance covers:
The ship itself, including its machinery, against perils of the sea
Only the cargo carried on the ship
Only the wages of the ship's crew
Goods carried by road from the port to the warehouse
Marine insurance has two main branches: hull, covering the vessel and its machinery, and cargo, covering goods in transit. Inland road transit is covered under inland transit or cargo policies.
A public liability policy protects the insured against:
Damage to the insured's own building from fire
Loss of cash due to dishonesty of employees
Legal liability to third parties for bodily injury or property damage arising from its premises or operations
Fall in the market value of the insured's shares

Liability insurance covers the insured's legal liability to others. A public liability policy pays compensation to members of the public injured or whose property is damaged due to the insured's premises or activities.
Under a reinstatement value fire policy, a claim is settled on the basis of:
The cost of replacing the property with new property of the same kind, without deduction for depreciation
The market value of the property after deducting depreciation
The original purchase price of the property as shown in the books of account, regardless of when it was bought
Half of the sum insured, irrespective of the actual loss
Reinstatement value cover pays the cost of rebuilding or replacing with new property of the same kind and capacity, without a deduction for depreciation. A market value policy deducts depreciation.
A comprehensive (package) motor policy covers:
Only third-party liability as required by law
Only own damage to the vehicle, without any third-party cover
Only personal accident of passengers
Both own damage to the insured vehicle and third-party liability
A package policy combines own-damage cover for the vehicle with the compulsory third-party liability cover. A 'liability only' policy covers just the third-party portion required by law.
A company wants protection against loss of money caused by the dishonesty of its cashier. The most suitable cover is:
Burglary insurance
Fidelity guarantee insurance
Money-in-transit insurance
Public liability insurance

Fidelity guarantee insurance indemnifies an employer for financial loss caused by fraud or dishonesty of employees. Burglary and money-in-transit covers deal with outsiders' theft, not employee dishonesty.

Securities Market Basics.overview: This chapter introduces the Indian securities market: the primary market where companies raise capital through IPOs, FPOs and rights issues, and the secondary market where existing securities trade on stock exchanges. It covers types of securities (equity, preference shares, debentures, ETFs), the role of indices such as Nifty 50, dematerialised holding, corporate actions like bonus, split and dividends, and basic market terminology. When revising, be clear on how each corporate action changes the number of shares and the price, how free-float capitalisation is computed, and how primary and secondary markets differ in purpose.
questions: A company with 100 crore shares trading at ₹250 has promoters holding 60%. Assuming the entire non-promoter holding is free float, its free-float market capitalisation is:
₹25,000 crore
₹6,000 crore
₹15,000 crore
₹10,000 crore
Free-float shares = 40% of 100 crore = 40 crore. Multiplying by ₹250 gives ₹10,000 crore. ₹25,000 crore is full market capitalisation and ₹15,000 crore wrongly uses the promoter stake.
An investor holds 200 shares of face value ₹10 bought at ₹900. The company splits each share into five shares of face value ₹2. Ignoring market movement, after the split the investor holds:
200 shares worth about ₹180 each
1,000 shares worth about ₹180 each
1,000 shares worth about ₹900 each
40 shares worth about ₹4,500 each
A 1:5 split multiplies the number of shares by five (200 × 5 = 1,000) and divides the price by five (₹900 ÷ 5 = ₹180). Total investment value remains unchanged at ₹1,80,000.
Which of the following is a secondary market transaction?
An investor buys shares of a listed bank from another investor through the exchange
A company allots shares to applicants in its initial public offer
A listed company places fresh shares with institutions through a qualified institutional placement
A listed company issues additional shares to existing holders in a rights issue

In the secondary market, already-issued securities change hands between investors, and the company receives no money. IPOs, rights issues and QIPs are all primary market issues that raise fresh capital for the company.
A bonus issue in the ratio 1:1 is announced. Which statement correctly describes its effect?
The company's total net worth doubles because new capital is raised
The face value of each existing share is halved to create new shares
The number of shares doubles, while reserves are capitalised and no cash is paid by shareholders
Shareholders must pay the face value in cash for each additional share received under the bonus issue

A bonus issue converts free reserves into share capital. Shareholders get one free share for each held, so the share count doubles, but net worth is unchanged. Halving face value describes a split, not a bonus.
Preference shareholders differ from equity shareholders mainly because preference shareholders:
Receive dividend only after all equity shareholders have been paid
Get priority over equity holders for dividend and capital repayment on winding up
Always enjoy full voting rights on every resolution placed before the company's general meetings
Have no claim at all on the company's assets on liquidation

Preference shares carry preferential rights to dividend and to repayment of capital ahead of equity shares. Their voting rights are generally limited to matters directly affecting them, unlike equity shareholders.
An exchange traded fund (ETF) tracking the Nifty 50 is best described as a:
Derivative contract that expires on the last Thursday of each month
Debt instrument issued by the exchange to track index returns
Fund whose units trade on the exchange throughout the day at market prices
Fund whose units can be bought only directly from the AMC at the NAV declared at the end of the day
ETF units are listed and traded on stock exchanges like shares, at prices that change during the day. Buying only from the AMC at end-of-day NAV describes ordinary open-ended mutual fund schemes.
Which of these investors is MOST exposed to the company's business risk?
A secured debenture holder of the company
A bank that has lent to the company against property
A fixed deposit holder of the company
An equity shareholder of the company

Equity holders are residual claimants: they are paid only after lenders and creditors, so their returns depend directly on business performance. Secured lenders and debenture holders have contractual claims and security, which reduces their risk.
A rights issue is offered at a price below the current market price. An existing shareholder who does not wish to subscribe can usually:
Renounce the rights entitlement in favour of another person
Demand that the company buy back the existing shares
Ask the exchange to cancel the rights issue for all holders
Convert the entitlement into a bonus share at no cost
Rights entitlements are generally renounceable, so a shareholder can sell or transfer them to someone else. This lets the holder capture some value instead of simply letting the entitlement lapse.

Market Participants.overview: This chapter describes who participates in the securities market and what each does: stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories (NSDL, CDSL) and depository participants, trading members, authorised persons, custodians, merchant bankers, registrars and transfer agents, and investors such as retail investors, mutual funds, insurers and foreign portfolio investors. Focus on the distinct role each intermediary plays in a trade's life cycle, who is regulated by whom, and which intermediary a client deals with for which service, such as opening a demat account or resolving a share transfer issue.
questions: A company wants an agency to maintain its register of shareholders, process transfers and send dividend warrants. It should appoint a:
Merchant Banker
Registrar and Share Transfer Agent
Depository Participant of the investors
Clearing Member

Registrars and transfer agents (RTAs) maintain the records of a company's shareholders and handle investor servicing such as dividends and transfers. A depository participant serves investors' demat accounts, not the issuer's register.
Which intermediary manages a public issue, prepares the offer document and coordinates with SEBI and the exchanges?
A merchant banker acting as book running lead manager
A trading member of the stock exchange on which the shares will list
A depository participant
A registrar to the issue

The book running lead manager, a SEBI-registered merchant banker, manages the issue process, does due diligence and files the offer document. The registrar handles applications and allotment, which is a separate function.
Which of these is primarily an institutional investor rather than an intermediary?
A custodian holding securities for clients
A depository participant opening and servicing demat accounts for retail clients
A stock broker executing orders for clients
An insurance company investing its policyholders' funds
An insurer invests its own and policyholders' money, so it is an investor. Brokers, depository participants and custodians provide services to other investors and are intermediaries in the market.
Who is responsible for the guaranteed settlement of trades executed on a stock exchange?
The issuing company
The registrar and transfer agent
The clearing corporation
The depository

The clearing corporation clears and settles trades and guarantees settlement through novation and its settlement guarantee fund. Depositories only hold and transfer securities in electronic form on its instructions.
A clearing member who clears and settles only his own trades and those of his clients is called a:
Authorised person
Professional clearing member
Custodial participant
Self-clearing member

A self-clearing member clears only its own (proprietary and client) trades. A professional clearing member clears trades of other trading members and custodial participants, which is the tempting but wrong choice.
An investor's shares are held electronically in a depository. Which entity actually provides the investor with account statements and executes instructions such as delivery instructions?
The registrar of the issuing company
The stock exchange on which the shares are listed
The depository participant with whom the account is opened
The clearing corporation of the exchange

Investors interact with the depository through a depository participant, which opens the demat account, accepts delivery instructions and sends statements. The depository itself does not deal directly with individual investors.
Foreign portfolio investors in India are registered with SEBI through:
Designated depository participants authorised by SEBI
The Reserve Bank of India's regional offices and the authorised dealer banks
Any trading member of a recognised exchange
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
SEBI has authorised designated depository participants (DDPs) to grant FPI registration on its behalf. Brokers execute trades but do not register FPIs, and RBI does not handle FPI registration.
A person appointed by a trading member to provide access to the trading platform as its agent, without being a member himself, is called a/an:
Sub-depository
Authorised person
Custodial participant
Professional clearing member

An authorised person is appointed by a trading member, with exchange approval, to offer access to the trading platform as the member's agent. The trading member remains responsible for the authorised person's acts.

Trading Membership.overview: This chapter covers how one becomes a trading member of an exchange, eligibility norms such as net worth and qualified staff, membership categories, the role of authorised persons, and the obligations of a member towards clients. Key areas include KYC and client registration, the know-your-client documents, risk disclosure documents, rights and obligations, segregation of client funds and securities, unique client codes, contract notes and the code of conduct. When revising, focus on what a member must do before accepting a client, what is prohibited, and how client assets must be protected.
questions: Before executing a client's first order, a trading member must ensure that:
The client has deposited at least one year's brokerage in advance
The client has completed a training course conducted by the exchange
KYC is completed and the client registration documents are executed
The client has opened a bank account with the same broker

Client registration, including KYC and the rights and obligations documents, must be completed before trading. There is no requirement of advance brokerage, exchange training or a bank account with the broker.
A trading member uses securities lying in a client's account to meet the margin obligations of another client. This is:
Prohibited, because client securities must be used only for that client
Allowed if the broker returns the securities within a week
Allowed if both clients belong to the same family
Allowed for retail clients but not for institutions

Client assets must be segregated and used only for the respective client's obligations. Using one client's securities for another's margin is misuse of client assets and is prohibited regardless of when they are returned.
The Risk Disclosure Document given to a client during registration mainly explains:
The tax rates applicable to the client's capital gains
The risks involved in trading in securities and derivatives
The list of shares recommended by the broker for purchase
The broker's own financial statements for the last three years
The Risk Disclosure Document informs the client of the risks of trading, such as price volatility and leverage. It is not a statement of the broker's finances, tax advice or a stock recommendation.
Which statement about a client's power of attorney or demat debit authorisation given to a broker is correct?
It allows the broker to transfer the client's shares for any purpose
It permits the broker to pledge client shares with lenders to raise the broker's own working capital
It is compulsory for every client before trading can start
It is limited to purposes such as meeting the client's own settlement and margin obligations

SEBI has restricted such authorisations to specific uses linked to the client's own obligations, and they cannot be made mandatory. Using them for the broker's own funding or any other purpose is prohibited.
A trading member receives a complaint from a client about an unauthorised trade. The most appropriate first step is to:
Ignore it unless the amount involved exceeds ₹1 lakh
Ask the client to approach the stock exchange directly
Record and investigate the complaint and resolve it within the prescribed timeline
Close the client's account to avoid further disputes

Members must maintain a grievance redressal mechanism, register complaints and resolve them promptly. A client may escalate to the exchange or SEBI's SCORES only if not satisfied, so referring him away first is incorrect.
Which of the following is a typical eligibility requirement for an individual or corporate seeking trading membership?
Being registered as a banking company with RBI
Holding a minimum of 1% of the exchange's shares
Having at least ten years of experience as a listed company director
Meeting the exchange's net worth and deposit norms and being a fit and proper person

Exchanges prescribe financial criteria such as net worth and deposits, along with fit-and-proper and qualification requirements. Holding exchange shares, banking registration or directorship experience are not general conditions for membership.
Why must each order entered on the trading system carry the client's Unique Client Code?
So that every trade can be traced to the actual client for surveillance and settlement
So that the exchange can charge a separate listing fee per client
So that the client's PAN is shown publicly on the order book
So that orders from clients get priority over proprietary orders
The UCC links each order to a registered client, enabling audit trail, surveillance and correct allocation. Client identity is not displayed publicly, and UCC does not affect order priority or fees.
A client wants to trade through a broker's authorised person. Who is responsible to the client for the authorised person's acts in relation to the business?
Only the authorised person, in his personal capacity, and never the trading member
The trading member who appointed the authorised person
The depository where the client's shares are held
The stock exchange that approved the appointment

The trading member is responsible for all acts of its authorised persons in connection with the securities business. The exchange approves the appointment but does not take over the member's responsibility.

Trading System & Orders.overview: This chapter explains the screen-based, anonymous, order-driven trading system used by Indian exchanges. It covers the order book, order matching on price-time priority, market types (normal, odd lot, auction), session timings, the pre-open call auction, and order types and conditions: market, limit, stop-loss, IOC, day orders and disclosed quantity. It also explains price bands and circuit filters. When revising, practise reading an order book, working out which orders match and at what price, and understanding how each order condition behaves when it is not fully executed.
questions: A trader places a limit buy order for 500 shares at ₹120. The best sell orders are 200 shares at ₹119 and 400 shares at ₹121. What happens to the order on entry?
500 shares are bought at an average price of ₹120
200 shares are bought at ₹119 and 300 shares remain pending at ₹120
200 shares are bought at ₹119 and 300 shares are bought at ₹121
No shares are bought because the full quantity is not available at ₹120
A limit buy at ₹120 can match only sell orders at ₹120 or below, so 200 shares trade at ₹119. The remaining 300 shares stay in the book at ₹120 because ₹121 is above the limit.
In NSE's trading system, when a passive order already in the book is matched with an incoming active order, the trade takes place at the:
Last traded price of the stock at the time of the previous trade
Average of the two order prices
Price of the incoming active order
Price of the passive order already in the book
Trades execute at the price of the order resting in the book (passive order). The incoming order may thus get a better price than its limit, which is why using the active order's price is wrong.
A trader holding shares bought at ₹500 wants to limit losses if the price falls to ₹470. Which order suits this need?
A stop-loss buy order with a trigger price of ₹530
A limit buy order at ₹470
A stop-loss sell order with trigger price ₹470
A market buy order placed immediately
A stop-loss sell order becomes active only when the price falls to the trigger, protecting the holder against further loss. A buy order would add to the position instead of limiting the loss.
An order with the 'Day' validity condition that is not executed by the close of trading will:
Be cancelled automatically at the end of the day
Be executed compulsorily at the official closing price of the day
Be carried forward to the next trading day
Remain pending until the trader cancels it
A Day order is valid only for the trading day on which it is entered. Unexecuted portions are cancelled by the system at the end of the session, not carried forward or forced to execute.
A seller enters 10,000 shares with a disclosed quantity of 1,000. What does the market see?
The order is hidden until the full 10,000 shares can be matched
All 10,000 shares are displayed, but only 1,000 can trade per day
Only 1,000 shares are sold and the rest are cancelled
Only 1,000 shares are displayed at a time and the next 1,000 show after each lot trades
Disclosed quantity reveals only part of a large order to the market. Once the disclosed portion is executed, the next portion is shown, until the full order is filled or cancelled.
Which of the following orders is placed to sell at the best available price immediately, without specifying a price?
Market order
Disclosed quantity order
Stop-loss limit order
Limit order
A market order carries no price and executes against the best available counter orders. A limit order specifies the worst acceptable price, and a stop-loss order waits for a trigger.
In the buy side of an order book there are bids at ₹305 (time 10:01), ₹305 (time 10:00) and ₹306 (time 10:02). An incoming market sell order for a small quantity matches first with the bid at:
₹305 entered at 10:01
The earliest bid, regardless of price
₹306 entered at 10:02
₹305 entered at 10:00
Price priority comes first, so the highest bid of ₹306 gets matched before the ₹305 bids, even though it was entered later. Time priority applies only between orders at the same price.
Why do exchanges apply price bands on individual stocks?
To guarantee that every order gets executed within the day
To curb excessive volatility by rejecting orders outside a permitted range
To prevent investors from placing market orders
To fix the price at which the stock must close every day
Price bands restrict orders to a range around a reference price so that sharp, possibly erroneous or manipulative moves are checked. They neither guarantee execution nor fix the closing price.

Clearing & Settlement.overview: This chapter covers what happens after a trade: trade confirmation, determination of obligations by the clearing corporation, netting, pay-in and pay-out of funds and securities, and the settlement cycle (currently T+1 for the cash market, with an optional shorter cycle for select stocks). It also covers novation, settlement guarantee funds, handling of shortages through auction or close-out, and the role of clearing banks and depositories. When revising, practise computing net obligations from a list of trades and understand the sequence of activities and who is responsible for each.
questions: A client buys 600 shares at ₹80 and sells 600 shares of the same stock at ₹82 on the same day in the same account. At settlement:
The client pays ₹1,200 as the trade is reversed
No shares change hands and the client receives the profit of ₹1,200
The client must deliver 600 shares to the clearing corporation and receive ₹49,200 in return
The client receives 600 shares and pays ₹48,000
Buying and selling the same quantity on the same day nets to zero securities. Only the difference of 600 × (₹82 − ₹80) = ₹1,200 is settled, received by the client as profit.
Netting of obligations by the clearing corporation means that:
Trades are cancelled if the member cannot pay
Profits of one member are used to pay losses of another member
Each member's buys and sells in a security are offset to arrive at one net amount to pay or receive
Every trade is settled separately and gross with each counterparty
Multilateral netting combines all trades of a member in a security into a single net position for funds and securities. This reduces settlement volumes, unlike gross trade-by-trade settlement.
Which entity moves funds between clearing members' accounts and the clearing corporation's account during settlement?
Clearing banks
Registrars and transfer agents
Merchant bankers
Depository participants

Funds settlement takes place through designated clearing banks, where members maintain clearing accounts. Depositories and their participants handle securities, while RTAs and merchant bankers have no role in funds pay-in.
Under a T+1 settlement cycle, if a trade is executed on a Thursday and Friday is a normal working day, the settlement takes place on:
Tuesday
Monday
Thursday itself
Friday
T+1 means settlement occurs one working day after the trade date. A Thursday trade is therefore settled on Friday, assuming Friday is a settlement working day.
'Pay-out' in the settlement process refers to:
Members depositing funds and securities with the clearing corporation
The clearing corporation releasing funds and securities to members entitled to receive them
A client paying brokerage to the trading member
The company paying dividends to shareholders
Pay-in is when members deliver funds and securities; pay-out is the reverse, when the clearing corporation releases them to receiving members, who then pass them on to clients.
If a buyer does not receive shares because the selling member defaulted on delivery and the auction also fails, the position is usually:
Cancelled with no compensation to the buyer
Carried forward indefinitely to the next settlement until the shares become available in the market
Settled by the depository from its own holdings
Closed out at a price determined under the clearing corporation's rules

When an auction cannot obtain the shares, the shortage is closed out and the buyer is compensated in cash at a close-out price set under clearing corporation norms. The depository does not supply shares itself.
Novation helps market participants mainly by:
Fixing the price at which all trades settle
Eliminating the need for margins
Removing counterparty risk between individual trading members
Allowing members to cancel their trades unilaterally even after the settlement is complete

Through novation the clearing corporation becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, so members are not exposed to each other's default. Margins are still needed because the clearing corporation bears that risk.
Member X, on behalf of clients, has bought 1,000 shares of a stock and sold 700 shares of the same stock in the same settlement (all trades for one client). X's net securities obligation is to:
Receive 300 shares
Receive 1,000 shares and deliver 700 shares separately
Deliver 1,700 shares
Deliver 300 shares
Net position = 1,000 bought − 700 sold = 300 shares to be received. Netting replaces separate gross movements of 1,000 and 700 shares with a single receipt.

Risk Management & Margins.overview: This chapter covers how exchanges and clearing corporations manage the risk of default. Key elements include capital adequacy of members, margins such as VaR margin, extreme loss margin and mark-to-market margin, upfront collection of margins from clients, exposure and position limits, price bands, market-wide circuit breakers, and settlement guarantee funds. Focus on what each margin protects against, how to calculate MTM losses and total margin on a trade, and how price bands and circuit breakers are applied. Numerical questions on margins and price ranges are common.
questions: A client short-sold 300 shares at ₹210 in the cash market during the day. The closing price is ₹216. The mark-to-market loss on this position is:
For a short (sell) position, a rise in price is a loss. MTM loss = 300 × (₹216 − ₹210) = ₹1,800. ₹6,300 wrongly multiplies 300 by 21 instead of the price difference.
For a purchase worth ₹8,00,000, the VaR margin rate is 10% and the extreme loss margin rate is 3.5%. The total of these two margins is:
Total margin = ₹8,00,000 × (10% + 3.5%) = ₹8,00,000 × 13.5% = ₹1,08,000. ₹80,000 is only the VaR margin and ₹28,000 is only the extreme loss margin.
A stock with previous close of ₹640 is in a 10% price band. Which of these sell orders will be rejected by the system?
Sell at ₹700
Sell at ₹712
Sell at ₹580
Sell at ₹640
A 10% band on ₹640 allows prices from ₹576 to ₹704. ₹712 is above the upper limit, so the order is rejected. ₹580, ₹640 and ₹700 all fall inside the range.
Mark-to-market margin is collected to cover:
The cost of opening a demat account
Potential losses in a future market crash only
The notional loss on open positions based on the day's closing price
The brokerage payable by the client
MTM margin covers the actual loss already incurred on open positions compared with the closing price. Future extreme moves are covered by VaR and extreme loss margins, not by MTM.
A market-wide circuit breaker is triggered by:
A member failing to pay margins
A single stock hitting its price band
The clearing corporation's settlement guarantee fund falling below its minimum required corpus
A sharp movement in a broad market index such as Nifty 50 or Sensex
Market-wide circuit breakers apply to the whole equity market and are triggered by large moves in the main indices, halting trading for set periods. Individual stock price bands work separately.
Why is the capital adequacy requirement imposed on trading members?
To fix the maximum brokerage a member can charge
To ensure that members have enough resources to absorb losses and meet obligations
To pay dividends to the exchange's shareholders
To decide the number of clients a member may register

Capital adequacy norms require members to keep base and additional capital with the clearing corporation, which acts as a cushion against losses and default. They are not related to brokerage limits or client numbers.
A broker allows a client to trade without collecting the required upfront margin, planning to collect it the next day. Under current SEBI norms this is:
Permitted if the client signs an undertaking
Permitted, but only in the cash segment and only for delivery-based trades of retail clients
Not permitted, and short collection of margin attracts penalty
Permitted for clients with a good track record
SEBI requires margins to be collected from clients upfront, and exchanges levy penalties on short or non-collection. Track record or undertakings do not exempt the broker from this requirement.
Value at Risk (VaR) margin is computed using:
Statistical estimates of the likely maximum loss over a short horizon at a high confidence level
The face value of the share multiplied by a fixed 50%
The dividend history of the company over five years
The book value per share of the company
VaR margin is based on the volatility of the security and estimates potential loss at a chosen confidence level (such as 99%) over a short period. Face value, book value and dividends are not inputs.

Legal Framework.overview: This chapter covers the laws and regulations that govern the Indian securities market: the SEBI Act, 1992, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and its rules, the Depositories Act, 1996, the Companies Act, 2013, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and SEBI regulations on insider trading (PIT) and fraudulent and unfair trade practices (PFUTP). It also covers investor grievance redressal and arbitration. When revising, map each law to its subject matter, know what constitutes insider trading and market manipulation, and understand the anti-money-laundering obligations of intermediaries.
questions: Two brokers repeatedly trade a thinly traded stock between themselves at rising prices to create a false appearance of activity. This practice is called:
Arbitrage, a legitimate trading strategy
Hedging, permitted for risk management
Market making, encouraged by exchanges
Circular trading, a manipulative practice under PFUTP Regulations

Trading among a group to create artificial volumes and prices is circular trading, prohibited under SEBI's PFUTP Regulations. Arbitrage and hedging are legitimate strategies that do not create false market appearance.
Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 'unpublished price sensitive information' includes:
The company's name and registered office address
The closing price of the company's share on the exchange
Information on a proposed merger not yet disclosed to the stock exchanges
Quarterly results already filed with the exchanges
UPSI is information that is not generally available and is likely to materially affect the price. Undisclosed merger plans qualify; filed results and public data are generally available information.
Under anti-money-laundering requirements, an intermediary must identify the 'beneficial owner' of a client account in order to:
Know the natural person who ultimately owns or controls the client
Calculate the brokerage payable on each trade
Determine the tax rate applicable to the account
Decide whether the client is eligible for allotment in the retail category of IPOs and FPOs
